# Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III
## Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III's Obituary
Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III, age 70, passed away on Sunday, March 17, 2013. He was born in Bay Shore, NY on March 27, 1942 to Edward and Jo (Walsten) Whelan Jr. He lived in the Muskegon area the past 46 years. Ed was a deputy for the Muskegon County Sherriff Department for 25 years, retiring in 2000. He also worked for the Egelston Township Police Department. Ed was a member of the Egelston Township Fire Department for 20 years and Fraternal Order of Police. He enjoyed fishing, hunting, camping and working in his yard. Ed is SURVIVED by his wife, Sandie; children, Kelly Whelan, Kimberly (Duane) Dailey, Edward (Shannon) Whelan IV, Kristi (Tom) Calhoun, Karen (Erie) Toney, Karla Tjapkes, Kevin (Heather) Houseman, Betty Jo Whelan, Michelle (Don) Krisatis, Erin Reznor, Jodi (Duane) Witham; 32 grandchildren; 20 great-grandchildren; brother, David M. Whelan Sr.; step-mother, Katherine Whelan; and his Harley Davidson. He was preceded by his parents; and wife, Barbara Ann Whelan. The Funeral service is 11 AM Thursday, March 21, 2013 at The Lee Chapel, 6291 S. Harvey St., (231) 798-1100 with Rev. Gerald Hagans officiating. The VISITATION will be 2-4 PM and 6-8 PM Wednesday, March 20, 2013 at the Lee Chapel. In lieu of flowers please make memorial contributions to Harbor Hospice.

# Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III
## Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III's Obituary
Mr. Edward Raymond Whelan III, age 70, passed away on Sunday, March 17, 2013. He was born in Bay Shore, NY on March 27, 1942 to Edward and Jo (Walsten) Whelan Jr. He lived in the Muskegon area the past 46 years. Ed was a deputy for the Muskegon County Sherriff Department for 25 years, retiring in 2000. He also worked for the Egelston Township Police Department. Ed was a member of the Egelston Township Fire Department for 20 years and Fraternal Order of Police. He enjoyed fishing, hunting, camping and working in his yard. Ed is SURVIVED by his wife, Sandie; children, Kelly Whelan, Kimberly (Duane) Dailey, Edward (Shannon) Whelan IV, Kristi (Tom) Calhoun, Karen (Erie) Toney, Karla Tjapkes, Kevin (Heather) Houseman, Betty Jo Whelan, Michelle (Don) Krisatis, Erin Reznor, Jodi (Duane) Witham; 32 grandchildren; 20 great-grandchildren; brother, David M. Whelan Sr.; step-mother, Katherine Whelan; and his Harley Davidson. He was preceded by his parents; and wife, Barbara Ann Whelan. The Funeral service is 11 AM Thursday, March 21, 2013 at The Lee Chapel, 6291 S. Harvey St., (231) 798-1100 with Rev. Gerald Hagans officiating. The VISITATION will be 2-4 PM and 6-8 PM Wednesday, March 20, 2013 at the Lee Chapel. In lieu of flowers please make memorial contributions to Harbor Hospice.

A $1.604 million contract awarded by the Hastings City Council on Monday will help Hastings Utilities change the way it collects and stores ash from the coal-fired Gerald T. Whelan Energy Center Unit No. 1.
Gathered for their second regular August meeting at the Hastings Municipal Airport Terminal, council members voted 8-0 to award a contract worth $1,604,531 to United Conveyor LLC, doing business as UCC Environmental, of Waukegan, Illinois, for a new fly ash silo and blower system.

# City Council approves key contract for Whelan 1 ash-handling system
#### Andy Raun
The contract covers material only. The construction project required to install the system is to be let out for bids later.
For many years, HU has moved ash out of the power plant by adding water to it to produce slurry, then piping it into a pond near the plant. Periodically, the dried ash slurry material then must be removed from the pond bed so it can be sold.
The new system, which will replace the sluicing system, will be compliant with the Coal Combustion Residual rule promulgated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The new system will allow for dry fly ash to be conveyed to a truck loading system and removed from the premises by a purchaser. Fly ash is a key ingredient in concrete and can be used in road construction.
The UCC bid accepted Monday is for a 120-ton silo equipped to receive air heater and economizer ash from the power plant in addition to the fly ash.
Blowers will be used to convey the dry fly ash, economizer ash and air heater ash to the silo.
Two bids were received, with various options addressed in each.
With supply chain lead times, the equipment for the new system isn’t expected to arrive until late spring or early summer 2025.
HU’s 2023-24 budget included $1.4 million for the new ash-handling system, but just $5,135 of that amount has been spent to date, the city Engineering Department reported in a bid evaluation memorandum to Utilities Manager Derek Zeisler.
The draft HU budget for 2024-25 allocates $3.1 million for the overall project, which is to include equipment, engineering and construction.
In other business Monday, the council voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-45 allowing the Community Redevelopment Authority to receive 2.6 cents per $100 of taxable valuation in property tax revenue for 2024-25 — the maximum tax rate a CRA is permitted, and in dollars and cents equal to $556,203 based on Hastings’ taxable assessed valuation.

# City Council approves key contract for Whelan 1 ash-handling system
#### Andy Raun
While the CRA’s property tax rate, or mill levy, for 2024-25 will be the same as it was for the current year (the maximum), taxation at that rate will generate $58,327 more in property tax revenue in the new year due to an 11.72%, year-over-year increase in the valuation, said CRA Executive Director Randy Chick.
“The levy’s the same, and we can’t go any higher,” he said. “Certainly we could go lower.”
Chick said the CRA uses property tax revenue to cover general administrative and legal expenses related to its work, as well as to strategically acquire and hold property in the city for redevelopment, clean up derelict properties as the need arises, meet state and federal grant match requirements, operate a revolving loan program, and otherwise address community needs.
The CRA currently owns 12-14 parcels of property around the city and plans to sell them them for beneficial redevelopment when the opportunities present themselves.
“When we acquire and hold property for development, we’re controlling our destiny,” Chick said.
The council also voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-47 authorizing a 1% increase in restricted-funds budget authority beyond the standard 2.5% increase allowed under LB989, a bill approved by the Nebraska Legislature in 1998.
Although the restricted-funds lid override involves budget authority only and no actual spending of money, under Nebraska law it can’t be approved without a council supermajority vote of 75%. In 2023, the council voted to approve the override by a vote of 4-3 — not enough of a margin to do so successfully.

A $1.604 million contract awarded by the Hastings City Council on Monday will help Hastings Utilities change the way it collects and stores ash from the coal-fired Gerald T. Whelan Energy Center Unit No. 1.
Gathered for their second regular August meeting at the Hastings Municipal Airport Terminal, council members voted 8-0 to award a contract worth $1,604,531 to United Conveyor LLC, doing business as UCC Environmental, of Waukegan, Illinois, for a new fly ash silo and blower system.

# City Council approves key contract for Whelan 1 ash-handling system
#### Andy Raun
The contract covers material only. The construction project required to install the system is to be let out for bids later.
For many years, HU has moved ash out of the power plant by adding water to it to produce slurry, then piping it into a pond near the plant. Periodically, the dried ash slurry material then must be removed from the pond bed so it can be sold.
The new system, which will replace the sluicing system, will be compliant with the Coal Combustion Residual rule promulgated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The new system will allow for dry fly ash to be conveyed to a truck loading system and removed from the premises by a purchaser. Fly ash is a key ingredient in concrete and can be used in road construction.
The UCC bid accepted Monday is for a 120-ton silo equipped to receive air heater and economizer ash from the power plant in addition to the fly ash.
Blowers will be used to convey the dry fly ash, economizer ash and air heater ash to the silo.
Two bids were received, with various options addressed in each.
With supply chain lead times, the equipment for the new system isn’t expected to arrive until late spring or early summer 2025.
HU’s 2023-24 budget included $1.4 million for the new ash-handling system, but just $5,135 of that amount has been spent to date, the city Engineering Department reported in a bid evaluation memorandum to Utilities Manager Derek Zeisler.
The draft HU budget for 2024-25 allocates $3.1 million for the overall project, which is to include equipment, engineering and construction.
In other business Monday, the council voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-45 allowing the Community Redevelopment Authority to receive 2.6 cents per $100 of taxable valuation in property tax revenue for 2024-25 — the maximum tax rate a CRA is permitted, and in dollars and cents equal to $556,203 based on Hastings’ taxable assessed valuation.

#### Andy Raun
While the CRA’s property tax rate, or mill levy, for 2024-25 will be the same as it was for the current year (the maximum), taxation at that rate will generate $58,327 more in property tax revenue in the new year due to an 11.72%, year-over-year increase in the valuation, said CRA Executive Director Randy Chick.
“The levy’s the same, and we can’t go any higher,” he said. “Certainly we could go lower.”
Chick said the CRA uses property tax revenue to cover general administrative and legal expenses related to its work, as well as to strategically acquire and hold property in the city for redevelopment, clean up derelict properties as the need arises, meet state and federal grant match requirements, operate a revolving loan program, and otherwise address community needs.
The CRA currently owns 12-14 parcels of property around the city and plans to sell them them for beneficial redevelopment when the opportunities present themselves.
“When we acquire and hold property for development, we’re controlling our destiny,” Chick said.
The council also voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-47 authorizing a 1% increase in restricted-funds budget authority beyond the standard 2.5% increase allowed under LB989, a bill approved by the Nebraska Legislature in 1998.
Although the restricted-funds lid override involves budget authority only and no actual spending of money, under Nebraska law it can’t be approved without a council supermajority vote of 75%. In 2023, the council voted to approve the override by a vote of 4-3 — not enough of a margin to do so successfully.

A $1.604 million contract awarded by the Hastings City Council on Monday will help Hastings Utilities change the way it collects and stores ash from the coal-fired Gerald T. Whelan Energy Center Unit No. 1.
Gathered for their second regular August meeting at the Hastings Municipal Airport Terminal, council members voted 8-0 to award a contract worth $1,604,531 to United Conveyor LLC, doing business as UCC Environmental, of Waukegan, Illinois, for a new fly ash silo and blower system.

# City Council approves key contract for Whelan 1 ash-handling system
#### Andy Raun
The contract covers material only. The construction project required to install the system is to be let out for bids later.
For many years, HU has moved ash out of the power plant by adding water to it to produce slurry, then piping it into a pond near the plant. Periodically, the dried ash slurry material then must be removed from the pond bed so it can be sold.
The new system, which will replace the sluicing system, will be compliant with the Coal Combustion Residual rule promulgated by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
The new system will allow for dry fly ash to be conveyed to a truck loading system and removed from the premises by a purchaser. Fly ash is a key ingredient in concrete and can be used in road construction.
The UCC bid accepted Monday is for a 120-ton silo equipped to receive air heater and economizer ash from the power plant in addition to the fly ash.
Blowers will be used to convey the dry fly ash, economizer ash and air heater ash to the silo.
Two bids were received, with various options addressed in each.
With supply chain lead times, the equipment for the new system isn’t expected to arrive until late spring or early summer 2025.
HU’s 2023-24 budget included $1.4 million for the new ash-handling system, but just $5,135 of that amount has been spent to date, the city Engineering Department reported in a bid evaluation memorandum to Utilities Manager Derek Zeisler.
The draft HU budget for 2024-25 allocates $3.1 million for the overall project, which is to include equipment, engineering and construction.
In other business Monday, the council voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-45 allowing the Community Redevelopment Authority to receive 2.6 cents per $100 of taxable valuation in property tax revenue for 2024-25 — the maximum tax rate a CRA is permitted, and in dollars and cents equal to $556,203 based on Hastings’ taxable assessed valuation.

# City Council approves key contract for Whelan 1 ash-handling system
#### Andy Raun
While the CRA’s property tax rate, or mill levy, for 2024-25 will be the same as it was for the current year (the maximum), taxation at that rate will generate $58,327 more in property tax revenue in the new year due to an 11.72%, year-over-year increase in the valuation, said CRA Executive Director Randy Chick.
“The levy’s the same, and we can’t go any higher,” he said. “Certainly we could go lower.”
Chick said the CRA uses property tax revenue to cover general administrative and legal expenses related to its work, as well as to strategically acquire and hold property in the city for redevelopment, clean up derelict properties as the need arises, meet state and federal grant match requirements, operate a revolving loan program, and otherwise address community needs.
The CRA currently owns 12-14 parcels of property around the city and plans to sell them them for beneficial redevelopment when the opportunities present themselves.
“When we acquire and hold property for development, we’re controlling our destiny,” Chick said.
The council also voted 8-0 to approve Resolution No. 2024-47 authorizing a 1% increase in restricted-funds budget authority beyond the standard 2.5% increase allowed under LB989, a bill approved by the Nebraska Legislature in 1998.
Although the restricted-funds lid override involves budget authority only and no actual spending of money, under Nebraska law it can’t be approved without a council supermajority vote of 75%. In 2023, the council voted to approve the override by a vote of 4-3 — not enough of a margin to do so successfully.
